title: Nuclear Receptors: Receptors That Are Transcription Factors

generated.pipeline: extract → Gemini draft → Claude Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: Estradiol, cortisol, and testosterone are {{c1::steroids}}, hydrophobic hormones built from four fused carbon rings made from cholesterol.
cards.quote: Estradiol, cortisol and testosterone are steroids: four fused carbon rings made from cholesterol (lipid synthesis).
cards.section: Finding the receptor inside the cell

cards.front: Why does a steroid hormone such as estradiol or cortisol need no receptor at the cell surface?
cards.back: Because a steroid is hydrophobic, it crosses the lipid bilayer unaided to reach an intracellular receptor.
cards.quote: Because a steroid is hydrophobic, it crosses the lipid bilayer unaided and needs no cell-surface receptor.
cards.section: Finding the receptor inside the cell

cards.front: When Elwood Jensen injected rats with tritium-labeled estradiol, almost every tissue released it while the uterus and vagina retained it chemically intact. What hypothesis did this refute, and what did it support?
cards.back: It argued against estradiol acting as a cycling redox catalyst and supported an intracellular binding protein in target tissues.
cards.why: A catalyst cycling between oxidized and reduced forms would be recovered partly altered, and nothing would need to hold it specifically in target organs.
cards.quote: Jensen recovered intact estradiol retained specifically by the uterus and vagina, pointing to an intracellular binding protein instead.
cards.section: Finding the receptor inside the cell

cards.front: A protein that binds DNA and controls whether a gene is copied into RNA is called a {{c1::transcription factor}}.
cards.quote: A transcription factor is a protein that binds DNA and controls whether a gene is copied into RNA.
cards.section: Finding the receptor inside the cell

cards.front: How does canonical nuclear-receptor signaling reach DNA differently from cell-surface pathways such as TGF-β/Smads or second-messenger cascades?
cards.back: The nuclear receptor itself binds both ligand and DNA as a transcription factor, requiring no second messenger and no kinase cascade.
cards.quote: Unlike TGF-β and Smads, where the messenger was the transcription factor, here the receptor itself is—no second messenger is made and no kinase cascade is required to reach DNA.
cards.section: Finding the receptor inside the cell

cards.front: What four modular parts are shared by most of the 48 human nuclear receptors?
cards.back: A variable front end (with AF-1), a DNA-binding domain, a flexible hinge, and a hormone-binding domain (with the pocket, pairing surface, and AF-2).
cards.quote: The human genome holds 48 nuclear receptor genes, and most share one four-part plan:
cards.section: One modular plan, forty-eight receptors

cards.front: In a nuclear receptor, the {{c1::DNA-binding domain}} is about 70 amino acids folded around two zinc ions (four cysteines per zinc) that sets one helix into the major groove to read six bases.
cards.quote: DNA-binding domain: about 70 amino acids folded around two zinc ions, four cysteines per zinc, setting one helix into the major groove to read six bases.
cards.section: One modular plan, forty-eight receptors

cards.front: How do the two transcriptional switching surfaces of a nuclear receptor, AF-1 and AF-2, differ in location and hormone-domain requirement?
cards.back: AF-1 sits in the variable front end and can work without the hormone-binding domain, whereas AF-2 sits on the hormone-binding domain.
cards.quote: Variable front end: differs most between receptors and carries AF-1, a switching surface that can work without the hormone-binding domain.
cards.section: One modular plan, forty-eight receptors

cards.front: A hybrid nuclear receptor joins the glucocorticoid receptor's hormone-binding domain to the estrogen receptor's DNA-binding domain in cells lacking both native receptors. Estradiol is added to Dish 1 and cortisol to Dish 2. Which target genes turn on in each dish, and why?
cards.back: Only Dish 2 (cortisol) turns on estrogen-responsive genes; Dish 1 turns on neither, and glucocorticoid targets stay off. The hormone-binding domain chooses the activating hormone (cortisol), while the DNA-binding domain chooses which genes are targeted (estrogen targets).
cards.quote: Estrogen targets: the hormone-binding domain chooses the hormone (cortisol) and the DNA-binding domain chooses the gene.
cards.section: One modular plan, forty-eight receptors

cards.front: Nuclear receptors identified by sequence resemblance before their small-molecule ligand was known were named {{c1::orphan receptors}}.
cards.quote: Most of the 48 were found by sequence resemblance before anyone knew their ligand (the small molecule a receptor binds), and named orphan receptors.
cards.section: One modular plan, forty-eight receptors

cards.front: Which cellular lipids act as ligands for the nuclear receptors PPARs, LXR, and FXR?
cards.back: PPARs bind fatty acids, LXR binds oxidized cholesterol, and FXR binds bile acids.
cards.why: Matching these former orphan receptors to cellular lipids showed that the nuclear receptor family also senses the cell's own lipid state.
cards.quote: Several have since been matched to cellular lipids—PPARs bind fatty acids, LXR binds oxidized cholesterol, and FXR binds bile acids
cards.section: One modular plan, forty-eight receptors

cards.front: Before hormone arrives, what two jobs do Hsp90-based chaperones perform for glucocorticoid and androgen receptors?
cards.back: They keep the hormone-binding pocket ready to bind ligand and hold the receptor off DNA.
cards.why: Hormone binding rearranges the complex so the receptor enters the nucleus, sheds its chaperones, pairs with an identical copy, and binds DNA.
cards.quote: chaperones (proteins that help other proteins hold their shape) built around Hsp90, which keep the pocket ready and keep the receptor off DNA.
cards.section: Two ways to wait—and how DNA spacing helps pick the pair

cards.front: Enucleated-cell and antibody-staining experiments showed that most unliganded estrogen receptor already sits inside the nucleus, even though it uses the same Hsp90 chaperones as cytoplasmic glucocorticoid receptors. What unifying rule does this support for steroid receptors?
cards.back: Steroid receptors are united by waiting off DNA with Hsp90 chaperones rather than strictly by waiting in the cytoplasm.
cards.quote: The estrogen receptor uses the same Hsp90 chaperones, yet 1984 experiments (on enucleated cells and with antibody staining) placed most of it inside the nucleus even before hormone arrives.
cards.section: Two ways to wait—and how DNA spacing helps pick the pair

cards.front: How does the pre-hormone waiting state of thyroid hormone and retinoic acid receptors differ from that of steroid receptors?
cards.back: Thyroid hormone and retinoic acid receptors wait in the nucleus on DNA, paired with RXR and holding co-repressors, instead of waiting off DNA with chaperones.
cards.why: When hormone arrives, it swaps the co-repressors for co-activators to switch the gene on.
cards.quote: Receptors for thyroid hormone, retinoic acid, vitamin D and the PPARs stay in the nucleus on DNA, paired with RXR.
cards.section: Two ways to wait—and how DNA spacing helps pick the pair

cards.front: Why is a gene bound by an unliganded thyroid hormone or retinoic acid receptor quieter than having no receptor at that gene at all?
cards.back: Without hormone, those receptors hold co-repressors on DNA, creating active repression rather than a neutral silent state.
cards.why: Active repression is best documented for thyroid hormone and retinoic acid receptors and should not be assumed for every RXR partner.
cards.quote: Without hormone, thyroid hormone and retinoic acid receptors hold co-repressors (proteins that keep a gene off), creating an active "off"—quieter than no receptor at all;
cards.section: Two ways to wait—and how DNA spacing helps pick the pair

cards.front: How does the layout of the two six-base half-sites differ between a steroid homodimer response element and an RXR heterodimer response element?
cards.back: Steroid homodimers bind an inverted repeat (head-to-head palindrome), whereas RXR pairs bind a direct repeat whose two halves point the same way.
cards.quote: For RXR pairs, the two halves point the same way, and the gap between them helps decide which pair fits:
cards.section: Two ways to wait—and how DNA spacing helps pick the pair

cards.front: A gene promoter contains a direct repeat of two six-base half-sites separated by a 4-base gap, which fits thyroid hormone receptor + RXR. A mutation deletes 1 base from the spacer, leaving a 3-base gap. Which RXR heterodimer is now favored to fit that site, and why?
cards.back: Vitamin D receptor + RXR is now favored. For RXR direct repeats, the spacer length helps decide which pair fits: a 4-base gap fits thyroid hormone receptor + RXR, whereas a 3-base gap fits vitamin D receptor + RXR.
cards.quote: For RXR pairs, the two halves point the same way, and the gap between them helps decide which pair fits:
cards.section: Two ways to wait—and how DNA spacing helps pick the pair

cards.front: Each nuclear receptor DNA-binding domain reads a 6-base half-site. How many total base pairs span a thyroid hormone receptor + RXR direct-repeat response element (4-base gap) compared with a PPAR + RXR element (1-base gap)?
cards.back: 16 bp for thyroid hormone receptor + RXR versus 13 bp for PPAR + RXR (3 bp longer). Setup: two 6-base halves plus spacer gives 6 + 4 + 6 = 16 bp and 6 + 1 + 6 = 13 bp.
cards.quote: Because most receptors act in pairs, their DNA site—a response element—has two six-base halves.
cards.section: Two ways to wait—and how DNA spacing helps pick the pair

cards.front: How do co-activators and co-repressors recruited by nuclear receptors modify chromatin to control transcription?
cards.back: Co-activators bring enzymes that add acetyl groups to histones to loosen chromatin for RNA polymerase, while co-repressors bring enzymes that remove acetyl groups to keep it tightly packed.
cards.quote: Tightly packed chromatin resists transcription: co-activators bring enzymes that add acetyl groups to histones (loosening packing so RNA polymerase starts), while co-repressors bring enzymes that remove them.
cards.section: Two ways to wait—and how DNA spacing helps pick the pair

cards.front: In cells without thyroid hormone, a drug inhibits the enzymes that remove acetyl groups from histones. What happens to active repression at a thyroid-hormone-responsive gene, and why?
cards.back: Active repression weakens and transcription rises. Unliganded thyroid hormone receptors hold co-repressors that rely on removing acetyl groups from histones to keep chromatin tightly packed; blocking acetyl removal opposes that tight packing.
cards.quote: Tightly packed chromatin resists transcription: co-activators bring enzymes that add acetyl groups to histones (loosening packing so RNA polymerase starts), while co-repressors bring enzymes that remove them.
cards.section: Two ways to wait—and how DNA spacing helps pick the pair

cards.front: A cell carries a mutant thyroid hormone receptor that still binds DNA and co-repressors normally but cannot bind thyroid hormone. What happens to its target gene when the cell receives a high dose of thyroid hormone, and why?
cards.back: The target gene stays held off regardless of hormone dose. Because the mutant receptor cannot bind hormone, it can never swap its co-repressors for co-activators.
cards.quote: Cell B's mutant can never make that swap, so it holds the gene off whatever the hormone level
cards.section: Two ways to wait—and how DNA spacing helps pick the pair

cards.front: Unlike hydrophobic steroids, thyroid hormone carries electrical charges. How does it still signal through an intracellular nuclear receptor?
cards.back: Thyroid hormone crosses the plasma membrane via transporter proteins, which act only as a door while the receptor stays inside the cell.
cards.quote: thyroid hormone, retinoic acid (from vitamin A) and active vitamin D use nuclear receptors, but thyroid hormone carries charges and enters via transporter proteins
cards.section: Two ways to wait—and how DNA spacing helps pick the pair

cards.front: A cell loses its plasma-membrane transporter for thyroid hormone while keeping normal nuclear thyroid hormone receptors. What happens to thyroid-responsive genes when extracellular thyroid hormone rises, and why?
cards.back: Target genes remain actively off. Because charged thyroid hormone depends on membrane transporters to enter the cell, it cannot reach the nuclear receptor to swap co-repressors for co-activators.
cards.quote: thyroid hormone carries charges and enters via transporter proteins—a transporter is a door, and the receptor stays inside.
cards.section: Two ways to wait—and how DNA spacing helps pick the pair

cards.front: In the complete absence of thyroid hormone, compare basal transcription of a thyroid-responsive gene in Cell X (thyroid hormone receptor gene deleted) versus Cell Y (carrying a mutant receptor that binds DNA and co-repressors but not hormone). Which has higher basal transcription, and why?
cards.back: Cell X (deleted receptor) has higher basal transcription than Cell Y. Resting on the active-repression rule, an unliganded thyroid hormone receptor on DNA holds co-repressors that make the gene quieter than having no receptor at all, so Cell Y actively suppresses transcription while Cell X does not.
cards.quote: Without hormone, thyroid hormone and retinoic acid receptors hold co-repressors (proteins that keep a gene off), creating an active "off"—quieter than no receptor at all;
cards.section: Two ways to wait—and how DNA spacing helps pick the pair

cards.front: A molecule that binds a nuclear receptor pocket and switches the receptor on is an {{c1::agonist}}, whereas a molecule occupying the pocket without switching it on is an antagonist.
cards.quote: folding over an agonist (a molecule that switches the receptor on) or swinging into the co-activator groove with an antagonist (a molecule occupying the pocket without switching it on).
cards.section: What the hormone changes: helix 12 and helper proteins

cards.front: How does helix 12 behave when the estrogen receptor binds estradiol (an agonist) versus 4-hydroxytamoxifen (an antagonist), and what does each position do to co-activator docking?
cards.back: With estradiol, helix 12 closes over the pocket to complete the AF-2 groove for co-activators; with 4-hydroxytamoxifen, helix 12 lies inside the AF-2 groove, excluding co-activators.
cards.quote: With estradiol in the pocket, closed helix 12 completes the shallow AF-2 groove on the domain surface, fitting the short LXXLL helix
cards.section: What the hormone changes: helix 12 and helper proteins

cards.front: Co-activators fit into the closed AF-2 surface groove of a nuclear receptor using a short {{c1::LXXLL}} helix, where L is leucine and X is any amino acid.
cards.quote: closed helix 12 completes the shallow AF-2 groove on the domain surface, fitting the short LXXLL helix (L = leucine, X = any amino acid) of co-activators.
cards.section: What the hormone changes: helix 12 and helper proteins

cards.front: A purified estrogen receptor binding assay compares unmodified tamoxifen with its liver metabolite 4-hydroxytamoxifen. Which binds more tightly, and how does its structure prevent helix 12 from closing?
cards.back: 4-hydroxytamoxifen binds more tightly and blocks lid closure with its long side chain. The liver converts tamoxifen into tighter-binding metabolites whose long side chain projects into the space where helix 12 would close, pushing helix 12 into the AF-2 groove.
cards.quote: The liver converts tamoxifen into tighter-binding metabolites such as 4-hydroxytamoxifen, whose long side chain projects where the lid should close.
cards.section: What the hormone changes: helix 12 and helper proteins

cards.front: AF-1 is deleted from the estrogen receptor while its DNA-binding domain and hormone-binding domain (with AF-2) remain intact. In uterine cells where tamoxifen normally activates a target gene, how does this mutant respond to estradiol versus 4-hydroxytamoxifen, and why?
cards.back: Estradiol still activates the gene, whereas 4-hydroxytamoxifen loses activation. Estradiol can still act through closed helix 12 and AF-2, while 4-hydroxytamoxifen blocks AF-2 and now has no AF-1 left to use.
cards.quote: Estradiol still activates via closed helix 12 and AF-2, whereas 4-hydroxytamoxifen loses activation because AF-2 is blocked and AF-1 is gone.
cards.section: What the hormone changes: helix 12 and helper proteins

cards.front: A chimeric receptor combines the estrogen receptor's variable front end (with AF-1) and hormone-binding domain with the glucocorticoid receptor's DNA-binding domain. It is expressed in uterine cells rich in AF-1-compatible co-activators and treated with 4-hydroxytamoxifen. Which genes turn on, and why?
cards.back: Predicted: glucocorticoid-responsive genes turn on, while estrogen targets stay off. By the lesson's modular logic, 4-hydroxytamoxifen binds the estrogen hormone-binding domain and blocks AF-2 while leaving AF-1 intact for the uterine co-activators, and the glucocorticoid DNA-binding domain directs the receptor to glucocorticoid response elements.
cards.quote: A tamoxifen-bound receptor still pairs on DNA with AF-1 intact at its front end.
cards.section: What the hormone changes: helix 12 and helper proteins

cards.front: Why does tamoxifen block estrogen signaling in breast tissue while imitating estrogen in the uterus and post-menopausal bone?
cards.back: Tamoxifen blocks AF-2 while leaving DNA binding and AF-1 intact, so tissues rich in co-activators usable through AF-1 turn genes on, whereas tissues with relatively more co-repressors keep them off.
cards.quote: A tissue rich in a co-activator usable through AF-1 reads tamoxifen as "on"; one with relatively more co-repressor reads it as "off."
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Tamoxifen keeps an estrogen-responsive gene off in a breast cell line but switches it on in a uterine cell line. Design a perturbation experiment in these two cell lines to test whether differences in co-activator abundance explain the opposite outcomes, and predict the results.
cards.back: Measure co-activators and co-repressors in both lines, then lower the candidate co-activator in uterine cells and raise it in breast cells. Resting on the rule that each cell's helper proteins decide whether a ligand-bound receptor turns genes on, tamoxifen should lose activation in uterine cells and gain it in breast cells, while estradiol still activates both.
cards.quote: Measure co-activators and co-repressors, then lower the candidate co-activator in uterine cells and raise it in breast cells.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A drug such as tamoxifen or raloxifene that acts as an agonist in some tissues and an antagonist in others is called a {{c1::selective estrogen receptor modulator}}.
cards.quote: Such a drug is a selective estrogen receptor modulator: neither agonist nor antagonist until you name the tissue and gene.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Beyond tissue differences in co-activators (such as SRC-1) and co-repressors, what two other differences are possible in how a tissue responds to estrogen or tamoxifen?
cards.back: There are two estrogen receptor genes, and ERK (from the Ras/MAPK pathway) can phosphorylate AF-1.
cards.quote: Other differences are possible too: there are two estrogen receptor genes, and ERK (Ras and MAPK) can phosphorylate AF-1.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: How does raloxifene's tissue profile differ from tamoxifen's, and what condition is it used to treat?
cards.back: Raloxifene acts like estrogen in bone without stimulating the uterus, and it is used against osteoporosis.
cards.quote: Raloxifene is a second example, acting like estrogen in bone without stimulating the uterus, and it is used against osteoporosis.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Why do canonical steroid responses build over hours while adrenaline via cAMP/PKA acts in seconds, and what two advantages does the slower route provide?
cards.back: Steroids require synthesizing new mRNA (tens of minutes) and new protein (hours); in return, new proteins outlast the hormone and one receptor resets many genes at once.
cards.quote: In return, new proteins outlast the hormone, and one receptor resets many genes at once.
cards.section: Why it takes hours, and where it meets medicine

cards.front: Cultured cells are pretreated with a drug that completely blocks new RNA synthesis, then stimulated with either cortisol or adrenaline (acting via cAMP/PKA). How does blocking RNA synthesis affect each hormone's canonical response, and why?
cards.back: Cortisol's canonical enzyme-level response is prevented, whereas adrenaline's rapid cAMP/PKA response still occurs within seconds. Cortisol works by generating new mRNA and protein over tens of minutes to hours, while cAMP/PKA acts rapidly without waiting for transcription.
cards.quote: the first new messenger RNAs appear within tens of minutes of the hormone, and the change in the cell's proteins builds over hours
cards.section: Why it takes hours, and where it meets medicine

cards.front: Why does long-term treatment with anti-inflammatory glucocorticoids such as prednisone or dexamethasone also raise blood glucose and thin bone?
cards.back: Because nearly every cell in the body expresses the glucocorticoid receptor, systemic drug treatment alters gene programs outside immune tissues as well.
cards.quote: Because nearly every cell expresses this receptor, long treatment also raises blood glucose and thins bone.
cards.section: Why it takes hours, and where it meets medicine

cards.front: A synthetic glucocorticoid allows the glucocorticoid receptor to tether to NF-κB without forming DNA-binding dimers. Which anti-inflammatory action could survive, and what two questions must still be tested before claiming side-effect-free therapy?
cards.back: Direct blunting of NF-κB at inflammatory genes could survive, but clinical efficacy and side-effect reduction remain unproven. Resting on the lesson's three glucocorticoid actions, tethering needs no DNA binding by the receptor, yet DNA-bound induction of anti-inflammatory genes (including IκB in some cells) also contributes, so both inflammation control and loss of glucose/bone side effects must be tested.
cards.quote: Direct blunting of NF-κB at inflammatory genes could survive because tethering needs no DNA binding by the receptor.
cards.section: Why it takes hours, and where it meets medicine

cards.front: Thiazolidinedione diabetes drugs such as pioglitazone raise insulin sensitivity by acting as agonists of {{c1::PPAR-γ}}, a nuclear receptor that drives fat-cell formation.
cards.quote: Thiazolidinediones such as pioglitazone are PPAR-γ agonists that raise insulin sensitivity; discovered by their effect in diabetic animals, their target was identified as PPAR-γ in 1995.
cards.section: Why it takes hours, and where it meets medicine

cards.front: An XY individual inherits a non-functional copy of the X-linked androgen receptor gene. Predict the gonads, external body form, and blood testosterone level in the complete form, and explain why.
cards.back: Internal testes, a female body form, and blood testosterone in or above the usual male range. Testes still form and secrete testosterone, but because the sole X-linked receptor copy cannot work, tissues cannot read the signal.
cards.quote: internal testes making testosterone that cells cannot read: the complete form produces female body form with blood testosterone in or above the usual male range
cards.section: Why it takes hours, and where it meets medicine

cards.front: An XY patient has internal testes and a female body form, but blood tests show very low testosterone rather than levels in or above the usual male range. Using the androgen-insensitivity model, does a non-functional androgen receptor explain this case, and why?
cards.back: No; the low testosterone points to a defect in hormone production rather than receptor unresponsiveness. Resting on the lesson's androgen-insensitivity rule, a non-functional androgen receptor leaves internal testes making testosterone in or above the usual male range that cells simply cannot read.
cards.quote: the complete form produces female body form with blood testosterone in or above the usual male range—itself a clue in someone with a female body form.
cards.section: Why it takes hours, and where it meets medicine

cards.front: An extract of rat uterus containing 0.50 mg of protein is incubated with saturating tritium-labeled estradiol, and 54 fmol binds to protein. An identical sample receives the same labeled estradiol plus a 100-fold excess of unlabeled estradiol, leaving 12 fmol bound to abundant low-affinity sites. Each receptor binds one estradiol. How much estrogen receptor is present per mg of protein?
cards.back: 84 fmol per mg of protein. Setup: excess unlabeled estradiol displaces saturable specific receptor sites, so specific binding = 54 − 12 = 42 fmol; dividing by 0.50 mg protein gives 42 / 0.50 = 84 fmol per mg.
cards.quote: Following Jensen's 1958 tritium study, David Toft and Jack Gorski (University of Illinois, 1966) extracted an estrogen-binding protein from rat uterus
cards.section: How the receptor was purified and cloned

cards.front: Cloning the human estrogen and glucocorticoid receptor cDNAs revealed close homology to the chicken viral oncogene v-erbA, whose normal cellular counterpart is a thyroid hormone receptor; v-erbA still binds DNA but cannot bind hormone. Combining this finding with the thyroid receptor waiting rule, how does v-erbA affect its target genes?
cards.back: v-erbA holds its target genes persistently off even when thyroid hormone is present. Resting on the waiting-on-DNA rule, a normal thyroid hormone receptor sits on DNA holding co-repressors until hormone swaps them for co-activators, so a hormone-blind viral homolog can never complete that swap.
cards.quote: homology to the glucocorticoid receptor and to the chicken viral cancer gene v-erbA—whose normal cellular counterpart was identified by the end of 1986 as a thyroid hormone receptor.
cards.section: How the receptor was purified and cloned
